title: Binary Search Tree: Insertion
directAnswer: Walk down the BST comparing the new value with each node: go left if it's smaller, right if it's larger. When you fall off the tree (hit a null child), that empty spot is exactly where the value belongs — create the node there. Recursively, return a new node when root is null, else recurse into the correct side and return root. It's O(h) time — O(log n) for a balanced tree, O(n) for a skewed one — and the new node is always inserted as a leaf.

remember.pattern: BST descent: compare, branch left/right, attach at the null spot
rules: Smaller values go **left**, larger go **right** — the BST ordering invariant.
A standard BST insert always lands the new value as a **leaf** (at the first null spot).
Recursion returns the (possibly new) subtree root so the parent's link gets **reattached**.
The base case `root == null` is where the new node is actually created.
Don't rebuild or rebalance — plain BST insert just hangs the node at the empty slot it found.
whenToUse: Building a BST one value at a time from a stream of inserts
Any ordered structure where you locate position by comparison and attach at a leaf
A warm-up before deletion, search, or self-balancing trees
antiSignals: You need guaranteed O(log n) under adversarial inserts → self-balancing tree (AVL / Red-Black)
Duplicates must be counted, not dropped → store a count field or define a tie-break side
You need order statistics → augment nodes with subtree sizes
remember.takeaway: BST insertion is binary search that ends in a creation: compare your way down to the null spot and hang the new node there. The recursion's 'return the subtree root and let the parent reattach' pattern is the same plumbing used by BST delete and many tree rewrites.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you understand the BST ordering invariant and can descend by comparison to the correct null slot, returning the reattached subtree.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Forgetting to return/reassign the subtree root (so the new node is created but never linked), or inserting at the root instead of at a leaf.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State that a plain BST insert always creates a leaf, give both the clean recursive form and an iterative parent-tracking version, and note the O(h) cost and why balancing matters under skew.

problemStatement:
Given the `root` of a binary search tree and a value `v`, **insert** `v` into the BST and return the root of the updated tree.

A binary search tree keeps, for every node, all smaller values in its left subtree and all larger values in its right subtree. You may assume `v` is not already present.
constraints: 0 ≤ number of nodes ≤ 500 (the tree may be empty)
The value to insert is not already in the tree
The BST ordering invariant holds before insertion
understanding: Find the unique position where the new value preserves the BST invariant — that position is always an empty (null) child slot reached by comparing the value against nodes on the way down. Create the node there and return the (possibly new) root so the caller's reference stays correct.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the tree be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. If root is null, the inserted node becomes the new root — that's the recursion's base case.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the value already exist?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The problem says values are unique. If duplicates were allowed, you'd decide a consistent side (usually right) or store a count instead of a new node.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the tree need to stay balanced?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — a plain BST insert doesn't rebalance. The new node is hung at a leaf, so worst-case height can degrade to O(n). Self-balancing trees solve that separately.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Where does the new node end up?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Always as a leaf — the first null child slot the comparisons lead you to.

examples.explanation: 6 > 4 → go right to 7. 6 < 7 → go left; 7's left is null → insert 6 there.
Empty tree — the new node is the root (base case).
0 < 4 → left to 2; 0 < 2 → left to 1; 0 < 1 → left null → insert.

approaches.name: Recursive Insert — Return the Subtree Root (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Start here. The 'return root and reassign' idiom is the cleanest and the most reusable.
hints: Where can a new value go so the BST invariant still holds? Compare it against the root: which subtree must it live in?
Recurse into the correct subtree. What does it mean when that subtree is null — where exactly does the value belong?
Base case: a null subtree means you've found the empty slot — return a new node. Otherwise recurse, reassign the child link, and return the current root.
approaches.complexityReasoning: You follow a single root-to-leaf path, doing O(1) comparison per level → O(h) time. The recursion stack is also O(h). For a balanced tree h ≈ log n; for a skewed tree h = n.
approaches.explanation:
Insertion is binary search that terminates in a node creation. At each node you ask one question — is the new value smaller or larger? — and descend accordingly, until you run off the bottom of the tree into a null slot. That null slot is the *unique* place the value can sit without violating the ordering invariant.

**The base case creates the node.** When the recursion reaches `root == null`, you've located the empty slot. Returning `new Node(v)` here is what actually creates the node; every level above just passes that return value back up.

**The return-and-reassign idiom.** Each recursive call returns the (possibly updated) root of the subtree it was given. The parent writes that return value back into `root.left` or `root.right`. On the way down nothing changes except the one null link at the bottom, which now points to the new node. Writing `root.left = insert(root.left, v)` rather than just calling `insert(root.left, v)` is essential — without the assignment, the new node is created but never linked into the tree.

**Why it's always a leaf.** Because we only stop at a null child, the new node has no children of its own at insert time — it's a leaf. A plain BST insert never restructures existing nodes.

**Cost.** The work is proportional to the path length from root to the insertion point, i.e. the height h. Balanced trees give O(log n); a degenerate, sorted-input tree degrades to O(n), which motivates self-balancing variants.
approaches.insight: The 'recurse, reassign the child link, return the subtree root' pattern handles insert, delete, and many tree rewrites uniformly. The assignment is the part beginners drop — say it out loud: 'the child link gets rebound to whatever the recursion returns.'

approaches.name: Iterative Insert — Track the Parent
approaches.whenToMention: Offer if recursion is discouraged or to show you can manage the parent link explicitly.
hints: Walk down with two pointers: the current node and its parent. When current becomes null, the parent is where you attach.
Remember which side you descended (left or right) so you attach the new node on the correct side of the parent.
Handle the empty-tree case separately: if root is null, the new node is simply the root.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single descent along one root-to-leaf path → O(h) time. Only a couple of pointers are kept → O(1) extra space (no recursion stack).
approaches.explanation:
The iterative version makes the descent explicit and uses no call stack, so its extra space is O(1).

**Two pointers and a side.** Keep `cur` (the node you're examining) and `parent` (the node above it). At each step compare `v` with `cur.data`: if smaller, remember you went left and move `cur = cur.left`; otherwise remember right and move `cur = cur.right`. When `cur` becomes null you've found the empty slot, and `parent` is the node that should adopt the new leaf.

**Attach on the recorded side.** You must remember whether the final step went left or right, because once `cur` is null you can't tell. With that boolean (or by re-comparing `v` against `parent.data`), set `parent.left` or `parent.right` to the new node.

**The empty-tree special case.** If the tree starts empty, there's no parent to attach to — the new node is the root, so handle that before the loop. This is the one branch the recursive version folds neatly into its base case but the iterative version must spell out.

**Same shape as the recursion.** Both follow one root-to-leaf path; the iterative form just replaces the implicit call-stack bookkeeping with an explicit parent pointer, trading O(h) stack space for O(1).
approaches.insight: Iterative tree insertion is the 'trailing pointer' technique: keep a parent one step behind the current node so that when current falls off the tree, you still hold the node to attach to. The same trailing-pointer idea reappears in linked-list deletion.

dryRun.intro: Advance cur while remembering parent and the side taken. Stop when cur is null.

code.python:
def insert(root: Node, v: int) -> Node:
    node = Node(v)
    if root is None:                        # empty tree -> new node is root
        return node
    parent = None
    cur = root
    go_left = False
    while cur is not None:                   # descend to a null slot
        parent = cur
        if v < cur.data:
            cur = cur.left
            go_left = True
        else:
            cur = cur.right
            go_left = False
    if go_left:
        parent.left = node                   # attach on the recorded side
    else:
        parent.right = node
    return root

Trailing pointer — parent stays one step behind cur.
Descend left and record the side so we attach correctly later.
Hang the new leaf on the side we last descended.

edgeCases.behavior: root null → return the new node directly.
Descends fully left; parent is the leftmost node, side=left.
Descends fully right; attaches as the rightmost leaf.

pitfalls: Forgetting the empty-tree check — parent stays null and you NPE on attach.
Not recording which side you descended — you can't tell after cur is null.
Re-deriving the side incorrectly (e.g. using < where the descent used <=).

commonMistakes: Not reassigning root.left/root.right to the recursion's return — the node is created but orphaned.
Trying to insert at the root or an internal node instead of a leaf slot.
Ignoring the empty-tree case in the iterative version (null parent).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Calling insert without reassigning the link
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you call insert(root.left, v) but don't store the result back into root.left, the new node is created in the base case and immediately discarded — the tree is unchanged.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing empty-tree handling (iterative)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When root is null there is no parent to attach to; the loop body would dereference a null parent. Handle the empty tree before descending.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
def insert(root, v):
    node = Node(v)
    parent, cur = None, root
    while cur:
        ...
    # parent is still None if tree was empty -> crash
    parent.left = node

patternNote: BST descent by comparison terminating in a node creation. The recursive 'return the subtree root and let the parent reassign the child link' idiom is the shared plumbing for BST insert, delete, and search; the iterative trailing-parent-pointer version trades stack space for O(1) extra space. Cost is O(h), motivating self-balancing trees under skew.
